title: Fission
lead: Splitting a heavy nucleus into two medium-mass fragments releases energy, and a neutron absorbed by the nucleus can set it off. Because fission also frees neutrons, it can sustain a chain reaction, which reactors keep under control and which can breed new fuel.
objectives: Discuss how fission fuel reacts and describe what it produces.
Describe controlled and uncontrolled chain reactions.
summary_html:
• Nuclear fission is a reaction in which a nucleus is split.
  • Fission releases energy when heavy nuclei are split into medium-mass nuclei.
  • Self-sustained fission is possible, because neutron-induced fission also produces neutrons that can induce other fissions, $n+{}^{A}\text{X}\to \text{FF}_{1}+\text{FF}_{2}+xn$, where $\text{FF}_{1}$ and $\text{FF}_{2}$ are the two daughter nuclei, or fission fragments, and $x$ is the number of neutrons produced.
  • A minimum mass, called the critical mass, should be present to achieve criticality.
  • More than a critical mass can produce supercriticality.
  • The production of new or different isotopes (especially ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$) by nuclear transformation is called breeding, and reactors designed for this purpose are called breeder reactors.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 32.21) Neutron-induced fission is shown. First, energy is put into this large nucleus when it absorbs a neutron. Acting like a struck liquid drop, the nucleus deforms and begins to narrow in the middle. Since fewer nucleons are in contact, the repulsive Coulomb force is able to break the nucleus into two parts with some neutrons also flying away. (Figure 32.22) A chain reaction can produce self-sustained fission if each fission produces enough neutrons to induce at least one more fission. This depends on several factors, including how many neutrons are produced in an average fission and how easy it is to make a particular type of nuclide fission.

A pressurized water reactor is cleverly designed to control the fission of large amounts of ²³⁵U, while using the heat produced in the fission reaction to create steam for generating electrical energy. Control rods adjust neutron flux so that criticality is obtained, but not exceeded. In case the reactor overheats and boils the water away, the chain reaction terminates, because water is needed to thermalize the neutrons. This inherent safety feature can be overwhelmed in extreme circumstances.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following statements about nuclear fission is true?

options: No new elements can be produced in a fission reaction.
Energy released in fission reactions is generally less than that from fusion reactions.
In a fission reaction, two light nuclei are combined into a heavier one.
Fission reactions can be explained on the basis of the conservation of mass-energy.
answer.hint: Think about what the fragments of a split uranium nucleus are, and where the energy released comes from.

exercises.prompt:
What is the energy obtained when 10 g of mass is converted to energy with an efficiency of 70%?
(a) $3.93\times 10^{27}$ MeV
(b) $3.93\times 10^{30}$ MeV
(c) $5.23\times 10^{27}$ MeV
(d) $5.23\times 10^{30}$ MeV

answer.solution: Find the rest energy of the mass with $\kE = mc^{2}$, using $m = 0.010\ \text{kg}$ and $\kc = 3.00\times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$, which gives an energy in joules. Take 70% of it for the energy obtained, then convert to MeV with $1\ \text{MeV} = 1.60\times 10^{-13}\ \text{J}$ and compare with the options; the power of ten is the first thing to check.

exercises.prompt: In a neutron-induced fission reaction of ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$, which of the following is produced along with ${}^{96}\text{Sr}$ and four neutrons?

answer.hint: Balance the nucleons, counting the incoming neutron and the four that leave, and balance the charge: plutonium has $Z = 94$ and strontium $Z = 38$.

exercises.prompt:
When ${}^{235}\text{U}$ is bombarded with one neutron, the following fission reaction occurs: ${}_{92}^{235}\text{U}+n\to {}_{56}^{141}\text{Ba}+{}_{y}^{92}\text{Kr}+xn$.
(a) Find the values for $x$ and $y$.
(b) Assuming that the mass of ${}^{235}\text{U}$ is 235.04 u, the mass of ${}^{141}\text{Ba}$ is 140.91 u, the mass of ${}^{92}\text{Kr}$ is 91.93 u, and the mass of $n$ is 1.01 u, a student calculates the energy released in the fission reaction as $2.689\times 10^{-8}$, but forgets to write the unit. Find the correct unit and convert the answer to MeV.

answer.solution: (a) Charge is conserved, so $92 + 0 = 56 + y$ fixes $y$. The total number of nucleons is conserved too, so $235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + x$ fixes $x$. (b) The mass destroyed is the mass of ${}^{235}\text{U}$ and the incoming neutron less the masses of the products, about 0.2 u. Ask which unit of energy makes $(\kdm)\kc^{2}$ with $\kdm$ in kilograms and $\kc$ in m/s come out near $10^{-8}$, then convert that energy to MeV with $1\ \text{MeV} = 1.60\times 10^{-13}\ \text{J}$ and check it against $(\kdm)(931.5\ \text{MeV/u})$.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the fission of heavy nuclei releases energy. Similarly, why is it that energy input is required to fission light nuclei?

answer.solution: Read it off the curve of $\kBE/A$. Heavy nuclei have about 7.6 MeV per nucleon, while medium-mass nuclei have about 8.6 MeV per nucleon, so splitting a heavy nucleus into medium-mass fragments leaves its nucleons more tightly bound: the products have less mass, and the mass destroyed is released as energy. For light nuclei the curve rises with $A$, so the pieces of a split light nucleus would have a smaller $\kBE/A$ than the nucleus itself; they would have more mass than it did, and that mass must be supplied as energy.

exercises.prompt: Explain, in terms of conservation of momentum and energy, why collisions of neutrons with protons will thermalize neutrons better than collisions with oxygen.

answer.solution: Think of each collision as elastic. When a moving body strikes a stationary one of equal mass head on, momentum and kinetic energy can both be conserved only if the first stops and the second carries everything away, so a neutron can lose nearly all its energy to a proton in one collision. When it strikes a nucleus about sixteen times more massive, such as oxygen, it bounces back with most of its speed, as a ball does from a wall, and gives up only a small fraction of its energy. It therefore takes far fewer collisions with protons to slow a neutron to thermal energies.

exercises.prompt: The ruins of the Chernobyl reactor are enclosed in a huge concrete structure built around it after the accident. Some rain penetrates the building in winter, and radioactivity from the building increases. What does this imply is happening inside?

answer.solution: Ask what water does to a chain reaction. Water thermalizes neutrons, and slow neutrons are the ones ${}^{235}\text{U}$ absorbs and fissions with. If radioactivity rises when water gets in, the water is moderating the neutrons in the remaining fuel enough that more of them cause fission: the fuel inside is close to being critical, and the extra fissions make fresh radioactive fission products.

exercises.prompt: Since the uranium or plutonium nucleus fissions into several fission fragments whose mass distribution covers a wide range of pieces, would you expect more residual radioactivity from fission than fusion? Explain.

answer.solution: Yes. The fission fragments are medium-mass nuclei that keep roughly the neutron-to-proton ratio of the heavy parent, which is too high for stable nuclei of their size, so most of them are radioactive and $\beta^{-}$ decay, often through several steps, and because fission makes a wide range of fragments there are many different radioactive nuclides with many half-lives. Fusion of light nuclei makes mostly stable products such as helium; its radioactivity comes chiefly from tritium and from neutrons activating the surrounding material.

exercises.prompt: The core of a nuclear reactor generates a large amount of thermal energy from the decay of fission products, even when the power-producing fission chain reaction is turned off. Would this residual heat be greatest after the reactor has run for a long time or short time? What if the reactor has been shut down for months?

answer.solution: Ask how many radioactive fission products are present. The longer the reactor runs, the more fission products accumulate, including the long-lived ones, so the residual heat at shutdown is greatest after a long run. After shutdown no new fission products are made, and each one decays away on its own half-life, so the residual heat falls with time; after months the short-lived products are gone and only the long-lived ones, with their lower activity, still heat the core.

exercises.prompt: How can a nuclear reactor contain many critical masses and not go supercritical? What methods are used to control the fission in the reactor?

answer.solution: A critical mass is the least fuel that sustains a chain reaction when nothing else absorbs the neutrons. A reactor holds many critical masses, but control rods made of nuclides that absorb neutrons strongly are placed among the fuel, so that on average only one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another. Moving the rods in or out adjusts the neutron flux to hold criticality without exceeding it, and the water that thermalizes the neutrons gives negative feedback: if it overheats and boils away, the chain reaction stops.

exercises.prompt: Why can heavy nuclei with odd numbers of neutrons be induced to fission with thermal neutrons, whereas those with even numbers of neutrons require more energy input to induce fission?

answer.solution: The nuclear force binds an even number of neutrons more strongly than an odd number. A neutron absorbed by a nucleus with an odd number makes the number even, so about 2 MeV more energy is deposited than when the number was already even. That extra energy deforms the nucleus enough to fission even when the neutron brought almost no kinetic energy; a nucleus with an even number of neutrons gets less, and the neutron must bring the difference as kinetic energy.

exercises.prompt: Why is a conventional fission nuclear reactor not able to explode as a bomb?

answer.solution: Ask what a bomb needs that a reactor does not have. A bomb must become strongly supercritical with fast neutrons, in highly enriched fuel, before it blows itself apart. A conventional reactor's fuel is only slightly enriched, so it can sustain a chain reaction only with neutrons that water has thermalized; if the reactor overheats and the water boils away, the moderation is lost and the chain reaction stops. It can overheat and melt or burst from steam pressure, but it cannot sustain the rapid fast-neutron chain reaction of a nuclear explosion.

exercises.prompt:
(a) Calculate the energy released in the neutron-induced fission (similar to the spontaneous fission in Example 32.3)
$n+{}^{238}\text{U}\to {}^{96}\text{Sr}+{}^{140}\text{Xe}+3n,$
given $m({}^{96}\text{Sr})=95.921750\ \text{u}$ and $m({}^{140}\text{Xe})=139.92164$. (b) This result is about 6 MeV greater than the result for spontaneous fission. Why? (c) Confirm that the total number of nucleons and total charge are conserved in this reaction.

answer.hint: Add the incoming neutron's mass to the mass of ${}^{238}\text{U}$ from Example 32.3, subtract the masses of the products, three neutrons included, and multiply by 931.5 MeV/u.
answer.solution:
(a) 177.1 MeV
(b) Because the gain of an external neutron yields about 6 MeV, which is the average $BE/A$ for heavy nuclei.
(c) $A=1+238=96+140+1+1+1,\; Z=92=38+53,\; \text{efn}=0=0$

exercises.prompt:
(a) Calculate the energy released in the neutron-induced fission reaction
$n+{}^{239}\text{Pu}\to {}^{96}\text{Sr}+{}^{140}\text{Ba}+4n,$
given $m({}^{96}\text{Sr})=95.921750\ \text{u}$ and $m({}^{140}\text{Ba})=139.910581\ \text{u}$.
(b) Confirm that the total number of nucleons and total charge are conserved in this reaction.

answer.hint: Take the mass of ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ as 239.052157 u. The incoming neutron cancels one of the four that leave, so three neutron masses stand on the right.

exercises.prompt: Breeding plutonium produces energy even before any plutonium is fissioned. (The primary purpose of the four nuclear reactors at Chernobyl was breeding plutonium for weapons. Electrical power was a by-product used by the civilian population.) Calculate the energy produced in each of the reactions listed for plutonium breeding just following Example 32.4. The pertinent masses are $m({}^{239}\text{U})=239.054289\ \text{u}$, $m({}^{239}\text{Np})=239.052932\ \text{u}$, and $m({}^{239}\text{Pu})=239.052157\ \text{u}$.

parts.hint: Use $m({}^{238}\text{U}) = 238.050784\ \text{u}$ and $m(n) = 1.008665\ \text{u}$; the $\gamma$ ray has no mass.
With atomic masses the electron's mass is already counted in the daughter atom, so subtract the two atomic masses.
Again the difference of the two atomic masses, times 931.5 MeV/u.

exercises.prompt:
The electrical power output of a large nuclear reactor facility is 900 MW. It has a 35.0% efficiency in converting nuclear power to electrical.
(a) What is the thermal nuclear power output in megawatts?
(b) How many ${}^{235}\text{U}$ nuclei fission each second, assuming the average fission produces 200 MeV?
(c) What mass of ${}^{235}\text{U}$ is fissioned in one year of full-power operation?

parts.hint: The electrical output is 35.0% of the nuclear power.
Divide the thermal power in watts by the energy of one fission in joules.
Multiply the fissions per second by the seconds in a year, then convert the number of nuclei to a mass with 235.04 g/mol and Avogadro's number.
